paper_title: PyroAdapt: Adapting Wildfire Prediction under Spatial Heterogeneity and Temporal Shift

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Prediction of wildfire occurrence is a rare-event problem compounded by spatial heterogeneity and temporal distribution shift, as fire occurrences are vastly outnumbered by non-occurrences, and predictor--fire relationship varies across space and time. Models trained on historical fire data may perform poorly under new conditions and require adaptation to the target distribution before operational use. We propose PyroAdapt, a pretrain--retrieve--rank framework that adapts a pretrained model to target conditions by retrieving historical locations with similar conditions and fine-tuning on the retrievals through risk ranking. For spatial adaptation, we condition risk on terrain, ecoregion embeddings, and fire rates, accounting for spatial context in the retrieval, and learn risk ordering from same-day fire--nonfire cell pairs. We compare direct ranking, residual pairwise DPO (RDPO), and selective ranking through a unified score-gap formulation that characterizes their gradient allocation. Over California (discretized into 666 0.25x0.25 grid cells), these objectives raise daily average precision from 21.62% for continued focal fine-tuning to 24.35--24.57%, and Top5% recall from 18.70% to 22.11--22.79%. Under a fixed daily detection budget of 34 cells (5% area), selective ranking captures 344 additional positive cell--days. For fires in the top 5%/10%/20% of dry matter consumption, selective ranking raises recall by 39.70/28.18/20.50 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, rolling evaluations over Yosemite show that the gains from ranking persist under temporal distribution shift. Together, these results show that PyroAdapt prioritizes the most fire-prone locations under a daily budget constraint and detects more extreme fire events.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Climate change is fueling more extreme wildfires (Abatzoglou et al., 2025), with devastating impacts on health (Qiu et al., 2025), ecosystems (Byrne et al., 2024), and the economy (Wang et al., 2020). Extreme wildfires are challenging to predict (Wang et al., 2022), as they emerge from the complex interplay of fire weather (Coen et al., 2018; Duane et al., 2021; Swain, 2021), terrain (Sharples et al., 2012), vegetation fuels (Rao et al., 2023; Swain, 2021), and human factors such as ignition and suppression (Keeley & Syphard, 2025; Kreider et al., 2024; Miller et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2023). Climate change further shifts the spatial pattern, seasonality, and distribution of fire weather (Jones et al., 2022) and fuel conditions (Baltzer et al., 2021; Ellis et al., 2022; Halofsky et al., 2020), so the predictorfire relationships model learns from historical data may not hold in the year it is deployed. Predicting wildfire occurrence can be posed as scoring each location on each day for its propensity for fire, conditioned on environmental covariates and spatial context (Jain et al., 2020; Kondylatos et al., 2022). Three properties of the data render this problem difficult. First, positive labels (fire occurrences) are rare, as most locationdays record no fire, yielding severe class imbalance and few positive labels relative to the volume of data (He & Garcia, 2009; Chawla et al., 2002; Liu, 2009). Second, the distribution of weather and fuel conditions changes from year to year (Abatzoglou & Williams, 2016; Jones et al., 2022), so inputs at deployment may come from shifted distribution.

Third, the mapping from covariates to risk varies across space, as terrain, vegetation, and ecoregion mediate how given set of conditions translates into fire risk (Parisien & Moritz, 2009; Hawbaker et al., 2013; Syphard et al., 2024). These factors compound: model must learn predictorfire relationships across heterogeneous landscapes from relatively few positive labels while generalizing to conditions not represented in the training record. Consequently, risk scores learned from past data may be poorly matched to the deployment year. We introduce PYROADAPT, unified PretrainRetrieveRank framework for batch-transductive adaptation using complete target-period covariates without target labels. Figure 1 summarizes the data flow. Historical focal pretraining initializes risk model. Unlabeled target inputs retrieve nearest labeled historical examples in standardized weather and spatial covariate space (Cover & Hart, 1967; Khandelwal et al., 2020). sections.title: 3 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Data-driven wildfire prediction. Data-driven wildfire prediction complements process-based models (Jain et al., 2020; Reichstein et al., 2019), using reanalysis and remote sensing inputs (Abatzoglou, 2013; van der Werf et al., 2025) to model fire risk at regional to continental scales (Huot et al., 2022; Kondylatos et al., 2022; Prapas et al., 2023). Our work studies how historically pretrained risk models can be adapted through retrieval and pairwise fine-tuning, with temporal evaluations of the Yosemite case and spatial prioritization across the domain of California. Long-tailed and cost-sensitive learning. Standard remedies for severely imbalanced wildfire labels (He & Garcia, 2009) include oversampling (Chawla et al., 2002), focal loss and class-balanced reweighting (Lin et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2019), logit adjustment (Menon et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2019), and decoupled classifiers (Kang et al., 2020). Cost-sensitive learning formalizes asymmetric misclassification costs (Elkan, 2001). Proposition 4 connects the binary-label RDPO preference-risk minimizer to cost-sensitive logit adjustment; weighted-focal control tests static reweighting. Adaptation under distribution shift. Importance weighting (Shimodaira, 2000; Sugiyama & Kawanabe, 2012), domain-adaptation theory (Ben-David et al., 2010), adversarial domain alignment (Ganin et al., 2016), and distributionally robust optimization (Sagawa et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2021) address sourcetarget mismatch. Test-time methods adapt with unlabeled target data (Sun et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021). Our approach instead retrieves labeled historical neighbors (Cover & Hart, 1967; Khandelwal et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020) conditioned on the target batch, making it batch-transductive (Vapnik, 1998) rather than source-only. Preference optimization and pairwise ranking. DPO reparameterizes preference optimization as closed-form loss (Rafailov et al., 2023), with extensions to alternative divergences (Azar et al., 2024) and unpaired objectives (Ethayarajh et al., 2024). Pairwise learning to rankRankNet (Burges et al., 2005), LambdaMART (Burges, 2010), listwise (Cao et al., 2007), and SVM-based (Joachims, 2002) approaches (see Liu 2009 for survey)optimizes inter-example order. RDPO compares reference-relative preferences over candidates. Its binary-label specialization, binary-label RDPO (Jiang & Sun, 2026), compares labels for one input and reduces to reference-centered classification

sections.title: 5 YOSEMITE: TEMPORAL SHIFT
sections.content: Setup. For the Yosemite case, we evaluate temporal shift on fixed 33 grid. The same nine cells appear in historical and target years, holding the candidate geography fixed while assessing year-to-year adaptation. We use daily GridMET meteorology (Abatzoglou, 2013) and GFED-derived dry matter (van der Werf et al., 2025) with twelve weather inputs. The main split contains 62,460 training griddays through 2020 (7,613 positives) and 3,285 target griddays in 2021 (363 positives). The historically pretrained TabNet (Arik & Pfister, 2021) is adapted for 100 epochs with AdamW at 104; retrieval uses = 5. The adapted local policies share the same retrieved rows, frozen pretrained model, initialization, and seeded batches. The main seeds are {11, 17, 23, 29, 37}; target labels are used only for evaluation. Full architecture and optimization details appear in Appendix B. We additionally train joint focal + direct ranking from random initialization on all historical rows, using the same 50-epoch Adam protocol as the pretrained focal model and direct-ranking coefficient of one. This from-scratch baseline does not use target-dependent retrieval; its full configuration is in Appendix B.2. The six local comparison policies are: the frozen pretrained model (no local adaptation), continued focal (local focal fine-tuning), weighted focal (Equation 23), direct pairwise ranking (Equation 3 at α = 0), selective pairwise ranking (Equation 4), and binary-label RDPO (Equation 17). All three ranking adaptations fix β = 1 and preference coefficient one, with no focal supervision or extra positive-label term (λ2 = 0). sections.title: 6 CALIFORNIA: STATEWIDE RISK PRIORITIZATION
sections.content: Complete-grid evaluation. California has diverse terrain, ecology, and fire regimes. This domain is discretized into 666 grid cells (0.25). Historical risk pretraining uses 20022021 data, and adaptation targets 2022. The fixed 20% historical sample contains 972,892 celldays. Batch-transductive = 5 retrieval queries all 243,090 unlabeled target covariates, yielding 363,643 unique historical examples for fine-tuning. Evaluation covers the complete daily grid, with 14,760 positives across 351 fire dates. The daily Top5% rule selects 34 cells per date, or 12,410 alarms in the 2022 evaluation. Within each of seeds {11, 22, 33}, adapted models share the pretrained checkpoint, scaler, and retrieved examples; pairwise variants use λrank = βrank = 0.1 and the same pair-sampling rule, with focal supervision excluded from all three ranking objectives. See Appendix for the full protocol.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: PYROADAPT combines historical risk pretraining, target-conditioned retrieval, and ranking adaptation without focal supervision. Over the entire domain of California, all three ranking objectives improve mean daily AP and Top5% recall over continued focal. At daily budget of 34 locations, the selective configuration captures approximately 344 additional neighborhood-smoothed positive celldays. Ranking also increases recall within retrospective high-DM strata at training-selected thresholds.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to help develop the theoretical framework, formulate mathematical claims, provide critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims, assist in the writing of proofs, provide feedback on experimental design, implement methods, clean and reformat dataset. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic data sets, propose or refine hypotheses, assist with translation, support qualitative and thematic data analysis, or interpret results. sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work involves no human subjects, no personally identifying information, and no new dataset release; all inputs are public environmental products (Abatzoglou, 2013; van der Werf et al., 2025; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, n.d.) whose licenses permit research use. Because risk ranking directs limited monitoring capacity, both error modes are costlya missed positive can leave developing fire unobserved, while false alarm consumes capacity another location neededso we report ranking, fixed-threshold detection, and top-ranked event recall separately (Section 2) rather than single headline number. Two risks deserve mention: location prioritization can disadvantage regions with sparse historical support, since our history features shrink such cells toward statewide prior, so deployments should audit performance by region rather than only in aggregate; and our label is neighborhood-smoothed occurrence indicator rather than verified ignition, so predictions should not be read as ignition forecasts. We therefore claim no operational readiness, and regard premature operational usewithout the deployment-matched evaluation of Appendix Eas the principal misuse risk of this work.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Theoretical claims are stated in Section 4 and proved in Appendix A, which also gives the expectedbatch coefficient qualification and conditions for order preservation. Yosemite data, architecture, optimizer settings, retrieval, policy definitions, seeds, and the rolling protocol appear in Section 5 and Appendix B, including the fixed-configuration table and initial gradient-norm checks. The California protocol is in Appendix D: label smoothing, the fixed 20% stratified sample and its data seed, causal history features with shrinkage and cold-start rules, retrieval distance, optimizer settings, stopping rule, XGBoost configuration, and training-only threshold selection; metric definitions, including pooled R@q versus daily Top5% selection and noninterpolated average precision, accompany the results. The protocol records pretraining epoch caps, fixed loss settings, and the exclusion of focal supervision from ranking adaptation. All datasets are public, and our code and configuration files will be released.

sections.title: B EXPERIMENTAL CONFIGURATION AND METRIC VERIFICATION
sections.content: B.1 YOSEMITE DATA AND ARCHITECTURE DETAILS The full Yosemite file has 70,491 rows from 19972022 and 9,219 positives. The nominal protocol starts in 2001, but no 2001 rows exist, so effective training begins in 2002. The twelve inputs are maximum/minimum temperature and relative humidity, precipitation, wind speed/direction, vaporpressure deficit, energy-release component, burning index, and 100-hour/1000-hour fuel moisture. Labels satisfy the supplied smoothed DM > 0; coordinates, time, dry matter, and carbon are excluded from inputs. Standardization fits only historical training rows. Retrieval uses the complete unlabeled target batch. The pretrained TabNet has widths 8, four steps, γ = 1.3, sparsemax, two independent/shared gated linear units, and virtual batch size 128. It uses 50 epochs, Adam at 5 103, and batches of 4096. Historical F1 selects each models classification threshold.

sections.content: B.2 FROM-SCRATCH JOINT FOCAL AND DIRECT RANKING The joint baseline initializes fresh TabNet with the same architecture and seed as the pretrained focal model and trains on the complete historical window. Its objective is Ljoint = Lfocal + E(x+,x) softplus(θ) + 0.05Mloss. (42) Focal supervision uses γ = 2 and positive-class weight 1 π+, where π+ is historical training prevalence. Direct ranking uses coefficient one and βrank = 1, with every positivenegative pair in each shuffled minibatch, including cross-date pairs. We retain the pretraining Adam optimizer at 5 103, batch size 4096, 50 epochs, and final checkpoint. The mask term remains zero. No reference scores, pretrained policy weights, or target-dependent retrieval enter joint optimization. Historical training F1 chooses its classification threshold; target labels enter only final evaluation. This tests one global joint-training configuration against subsequent local adaptation. Training data, optimizer, initialization, and update counts differ from the local policies, so the comparison does not isolate initialization alone or match total computation. The from-scratch joint baseline uses the same training schedule as the pretrained focal model; the local methods additionally perform 100 adaptation epochs. The initial-gradient analysis assumes pretrained initialization and therefore does not describe the joint baselines random starting point. The rolling 2021 results reuse the corresponding joint executions after verifying identical data windows and reference comparison checkpoints. B.3 PAIRWISE POLICY DETAILS All three local ranking configurations use β = 1, preference coefficient one, and no focal supervision during adaptation. Direct and selective ranking use every positivenegative input pair within shuffled minibatch, including cross-date pairs. Binary-label RDPO compares the true and complementary labels for each input, with no extra positive-label term (λ2 = 0). Each retains the same +0.05Mloss term, whose realized value is zero. The configurations share pretrained checkpoints, retrieved rows, seeded minibatches, AdamW settings, and 100 adaptation epochs. Their candidate definitions differ, so this comparison does not isolate only the cross-input reference target. No interpolation sweep is evaluated. The weighted-focal control retains fixed weights c0 = 2 and c1 = 2 + 0.1/π+ on the aligned focal loss. It is separate static reweighting baseline; it does not match the pure binary-label RDPO coefficients. Gradient matching is an auxiliary scaling control. The actual TabNet mask term is zero in these experiments, and AdamW approximately cancels uniform loss scaling; near-identical fixed/matched results should therefore not be overinterpreted as broad robustness result. For rolling, average the three test years separately within each seed, then compute t0.975,n1s/ across = 3 seed averages; the 2021 daily table uses = 5 seed scores. In 2021, 57 dates contain positives, of which 42 have both labels. With nine candidates per day, 0.05 9 = 1: the nominal daily Top5% metric is Top1 at an effective selection fraction of 11.11%. Mixed-day AP excludes all-positive dates. We report seed variability and paired directions without row-level significance tests. B.5 FIXED CONFIGURATIONS The 2021 local set has 11,187 unique historical rows and 1,582 positives (π+ = 0.1414), identical across policies and seeds. The TabNet group-attention matrix contains one all-ones group, yielding zero mask-loss term throughout training. The sparsity term enters the objective with coefficient +0.05.

sections.title: F DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Pretraining as foundation for adaptation. The evaluated framework uses historically trained risk model as the starting point for subsequent fine-tuning. All local ranking variants inherit its parameters and representation. Direct ranking optimizes positivenegative score gaps; RDPO and selective use frozen pretrained gaps to define alternative loss targets. California compares these targets at fixed pairwise settings, while Yosemite compares binary-label and cross-input preferences. Both experiments exclude focal supervision from ranking adaptation; their pair contexts, temperatures, and stopping schedules remain dataset-specific. The experiments support ranking adaptation from the evaluated checkpoints. The fixed-update continued-focal ablation isolates source selection and supports daily-AP benefit over matched random and full-history adaptation. It does not establish that retrieval is necessary, nor isolate its interaction with the ranking loss. Staging and pretrained-model quality are not separately controlled. The scalar-gradient analysis characterizes objective behavior under its stated assumptions, rather than establishing generalization guarantee. Deployment covariates and information access. Retrieval uses unlabeled deployment covariates, so the evaluation is batch-transductive. Californias primary protocol uses covariates from the entire target year before adaptation and evaluates all 666 cells on every test date. Although each row uses previous-day weather, adaptation sees the future target covariate distribution. Daily budgets specify the evaluation decision, not an online information protocol; issue-time adaptation using only then-available covariates remains unevaluated. The spatial pretrained model receives 26 raw fields, including an ecological category represented by learned embedding, and its causal history features draw on full historical label grids from prior years.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Evaluation scope. California evaluates one target year on locations present historically, so spatial heterogeneity here concerns temporal adjustment on fixed grid; unseen-region generalization and spatial feature contributions are not isolated. The reported seed variation measures training randomness conditional on the evaluated years. The three ranking objectives use common training-loss stopping rule but different realized update counts, which limits attribution of small differences solely to their targets. Fixed and dataset-specific ranking temperatures are evaluated configurations, rather than demonstrated optima from historical-forward sensitivity study. Yosemites fixed joint-training comparison changes data access, optimizer, and update counts, so it does not isolate initialization alone. Probability interpretation and calibration. Modern neural networks are often poorly calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). The no-focal ranking objectives optimize score gaps without constraining probabilities to be calibrated, so calibration is distinct from the ranking evaluation reported here. All reported California policies are evaluated without fitted calibration map. Deployment requiring probability estimates should fit and evaluate calibration on strictly forward historical predictions, separately from ranking assessment. High-activity diagnostic. High raw-DM strata are defined retrospectively for evaluation; training uses binary neighborhood-smoothed occurrence labels. The reported recall gains use policy-specific historical F1 thresholds and do not control alarm rates or demonstrate severity calibration. They support sensitivity to high observed activity under that threshold protocol. Positive celldays may share the same underlying fire and should not be interpreted as counts of independent incidents.
